title: Base Power Company: Chapter 3
gist: Base Power Company raised $1B at a $13B post-money valuation and has turned itself from a battery reseller into a vertically integrated Texas manufacturer: it killed its outsourced Gen 2 program, stood up its own factory and software stack in about 15 months, and now ships a 39.2 kWh 'Base Core' battery it claims is both the highest-capacity and cheapest residential system on the market. Utility partnerships have overtaken deregulated retail as the biggest demand channel (58% of July installs), Illinois is the second market, and the stated endgame is aiming the accumulated 'Capability Cannon' at the AI compute buildout to become the world's largest energy company.

insights.claim: Base Power Company raised $1 billion at a $12 billion pre-money / $13 billion post-money valuation in a Series D co-led by Ribbit Capital, Valor Equity Partners, Addition, and JPMorganChase's Strategic Investment Group, agreed on a Friday night and multiples oversubscribed by Sunday.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A roughly 3x markup from a $4B round about ten months earlier, closed in 48 hours, shows late-stage capital is chasing scarce revenue-generating energy hardware; expect comparable re-ratings across distributed-energy privates.
insights.locator: One Friday night earlier this summer

insights.claim: At $13 billion, Base is the second most valuable energy startup in the world behind Helion, and the most valuable one that actually sells a product today, despite being less than three years old.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Sets the private energy league table: shipping distributed storage is now priced above every pre-revenue generation moonshot except fusion.
insights.locator: $13 billion is, to be sure, a hefty price tag

insights.claim: The energy sector supports far more mega-caps than most investors assume: 18 energy companies are worth more than $100 billion and 55 worth more than $50 billion, with Saudi Aramco at $1.7 trillion and Exxon Mobil second at $650 billion, a full trillion dollars lower.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: The top-down TAM case for any energy entrant: the sector has room for many $50B+ outcomes, so the bull case never requires displacing Aramco.
insights.locator: Energy is an enormous industry

insights.claim: Today's largest energy companies were built around the winning assets of the previous energy system — oil fields, refineries, pipelines, tankers, centralized generation, poles and wires — so a shift in where the bottleneck sits opens room for a new entrant to reach the top of the list.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Argues incumbency in energy is asset-specific rather than durable; screen incumbents for exposure to assets whose scarcity value is eroding as the grid becomes the constraint.
insights.locator: This is a top-down view of the situation

insights.claim: The author explicitly discloses he is an investor in Base Power Company, plans to keep writing about it through and beyond an IPO, and closes the piece with a direct recruiting pitch to join the company.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Treat this as high-access primary-source reporting with an owner's bias: the operating data is specific and checkable, but the framing is unambiguously promotional.
insights.quote: That is certainly my aim with Base Power Company, which I’ve both invested in and plan to keep writing about through and beyond IPO.
insights.locator: In the intro to the last Ramp piece

insights.claim: The core strategic framework is that a company wins a large, old, incumbent-dominated industry by identifying the constraint holding it back, focusing everything on breaking it to capture a scarce defensible asset ('the High Ground'), then integrating outward from that position.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A reusable screen for industrial-startup investing: what is the binding constraint, who owns it, and can that owner integrate outward from it?
insights.locator: This is the question I tackled in Power in the Age of Intelligence

insights.claim: The durable asset a company like Base builds is not any single product but a 'Capability Cannon' — deployments, engineering, electrical services, manufacturing, brand, balance sheet, and policy chops — that can be re-aimed at each new opportunity so long as the remaining opportunity exceeds past accomplishments.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Implies underwriting the team's rate of capability acquisition rather than the current product's TAM, and explains why the company will look unfocused by conventional measures.
insights.locator: Collectively, Zach calls all the things Base has learned

insights.claim: Base's animating internal map of the power stack is 'Make, Move, Store, Sell' — generation, transmission and distribution, batteries, and retail/wholesale markets — and the company today occupies only the Store and Sell squares, with backward integration into generation and grid assets openly hinted at.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: The expansion roadmap is telegraphed; Ribbit has already published the same framework applied to both electrons and intelligence, so watch for Base moves into generation or transmission.
insights.quote: it’s really four things: you have to make it (generation), you have to move it (transmission and distribution), you have to store it (batteries) and you have to sell it (retail and wholesale markets).
insights.locator: The way Zach sees it, there are four things

insights.claim: Base's operating model is described internally as an expanding web where new ideas and scrappiness live at the edge and the center's job is to absorb what worked at the edge and standardize it into process and software.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A concrete test for whether a fast-scaling hardware company holds together: does it convert one-off heroics into encoded process, or keep re-solving the same problem in every new market?
insights.quote: “Imagine Base sort of like a web. It’s expanding outwards, and all of our new ideas are at the edge, and all the scrappiness is at the edge
insights.locator: Then she said something that describes Base in 2026

insights.claim: Base cancelled its entire outsourced Gen 2 battery program in April 2025 — one battery partner and two inverter partners — and redirected 100% of hardware and supply-chain engineering into a vertically integrated, Texas-manufactured Gen 3 that shipped as 'Base Core'.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: The single decision the company credits with changing its trajectory, and a template for when outsourcing a core component is the strategic error rather than the prudent step.
insights.quote: We made the decision to cancel our Gen 2 program and accelerate Gen 3, a lower cost, Base designed and manufactured (in Texas) home energy system.
insights.locator: On May 1, right on schedule as always

insights.claim: The head of hardware first recommended cancelling the outsourced battery program in May 2024 but was blocked because roughly $15 million in cancellation penalties would have consumed a large share of the money raised; when the company finally exited a year later it did so for only about $1 million in penalties.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A clean illustration of how a thin balance sheet constrains strategy, and how supplier penalty exposure can collapse by an order of magnitude once you have leverage and time.
insights.locator: He actually looked into canceling the contracts

insights.claim: The stated reason for owning the hardware stack is repairability rather than cost: a company that does not own its technology stack cannot fix the product when it breaks, and the team expected the outsourced design — more complicated than the prior generation — to break.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: The vertical-integration argument that actually holds in field-deployed hardware: iteration speed on failures beats bill-of-materials savings.
insights.quote: if you don’t own the stack of the technology, you’re absolutely not empowered to fix it when it breaks.
insights.locator: The idea of just canceling it kept nagging

insights.claim: The April 2025 'Liberation Day' tariffs made in-house US manufacturing more attractive and helped tip the internal decision to cancel the outsourced program, an example of trade policy directly redirecting a startup's capital allocation.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Tariff regimes are shifting build-versus-buy math for US hardware startups; expect more reshored vertical integration in energy hardware specifically.
insights.locator: right around April 2025, right when the Liberation Day tariffs

insights.claim: Base went from signing a lease on the old Austin American-Statesman press building in June 2025 to getting keys in September, running a pilot battery module line by January 2026, and having two production lines with batteries in the field by March 2026.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A roughly nine-month keys-to-production benchmark for battery assembly that resets expectations for how fast domestic energy manufacturing can be stood up.
insights.locator: Base people have their own definition of fun

insights.claim: By the end of 2026 Base needs to produce roughly 1,300 Base Core systems per week — about 5x current output, from a night shift plus uptime and cycle-time work — then 3x again the following year and 2x after that, implying roughly 30x today's daily production by 2028 in a larger, more automated second factory.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: The most falsifiable forward number in the piece; a 30x three-year manufacturing ramp is the key execution risk to check against each monthly investor update.
insights.locator: By the end of the year, they’ll need to be pumping out

insights.claim: The binding constraint has moved from the factory to the supply chain: Base has ramped its own factory faster than four or five key sole-sourced suppliers, and is now ramping more than ten supplier lines in parallel while embedding its own engineers on supplier floors to install tooling and manage the move from bridge to production suppliers.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Sole-source exposure across multiple critical parts is the near-term threat to the 5x ramp; watch for supplier diversification or further backward integration into components.
insights.quote: Basically, we’ve been able to ramp our factory faster than four or five of the key suppliers we’re sole sourced to right now.
insights.locator: When I asked Justin which team currently had the Turtle

insights.claim: Base deliberately kept its first factory manual to preserve design flexibility, on the principle that automation comes last because automation is inflexible, and only began integrating live controls for the factory's 21 robots in June 2026.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: An anti-pattern warning for capital-intensive hardware: premature automation locks in a product architecture that is still moving, stranding capex.
insights.locator: This is why automation comes last in Elon Musk’s five-step algorithm

insights.claim: Base Core carries 39.2 kWh of capacity versus 25 kWh for Base's own Gen 1 and 13.5 kWh for the Tesla Powerwall 3, and many customers install two units for nearly 80 kWh per home.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Nearly 3x the capacity of the market-standard Powerwall per unit changes per-home grid-services value and directly pressures Tesla's residential storage franchise.
insights.locator: Base Core is the highest-capacity battery on the market

insights.claim: The design deliberately packs cheap energy capacity into each home so that inverter, customer-acquisition, and installation costs — which are roughly the same whether you install 39.2 kWh or 20 kWh — are spread across far more kilowatt-hours.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: The real unit-economics lever is fixed-cost amortization per home, not cell cost, which structurally favors ever-larger residential systems over incremental Powerwall-sized units.
insights.locator: Base optimized for landing a lot of relatively inexpensive energy capacity

insights.claim: Base aims to roughly break even on the batteries themselves — charging members a few hundred dollars upfront to cover install plus a $19 monthly fee in some areas — and makes most of its money today storing power when it is cheap and selling it back to the grid when it is expensive.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Revenue is arbitrage and grid services, not hardware margin, so value scales with MWh under control and with price volatility rather than with unit ASPs.
insights.quote: Every battery is a time machine.
insights.locator: Base aims to roughly breakeven on the batteries

insights.claim: A new internal disconnect component called 'Disco' splits installation into two stages — electricians disconnect the home from the grid one day, installers plug in the module the next — cutting the install from three steps to two and reducing how much scarce electrician time each system consumes.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Electrician labor is the industry's real throughput constraint, so a design that de-skills part of the install directly relieves the scaling bottleneck.
insights.locator: The biggest change is to Disco

insights.claim: Base Core telemetry runs at 7 kHz on the Disco unit doing waveform analysis, versus 1 Hz on the prior generation and the every-five-minutes cadence utilities are accustomed to, letting the team diagnose and fix most issues remotely and near-instantly.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A multi-order-of-magnitude data advantage over utility norms is the raw material for grid-services and diagnostics products utilities cannot build themselves.
insights.locator: For Gen 1, sometimes people would call us

insights.claim: Base Core includes a 20 kW inverter the company believes is among the most American-made on the market, which matters commercially because the FCC has added foreign-made inverters to its Covered List over vulnerability to remote shutdown.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: National-security procurement rules are becoming a moat for domestic inverter manufacturing and a live risk for anyone importing inverters into the US.
insights.locator: It has a 20 kW inverter

insights.claim: In July 2026 Base signed over 6,000 new Battery members, roughly 40% more than June, while installing a record of more than 2,000 systems — more than three new members signed for every battery installed, leaving the company supply-constrained rather than demand-constrained.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A 3:1 backlog build is the clearest evidence the valuation is underwritten on manufacturing throughput, not on market demand.
insights.locator: In July, Base signed over 6,000 new Battery members

insights.claim: Base has batteries on over 17,400 customer homes and has deployed 585 MWh of storage, targeting more than 1 GWh by the end of 2026, with its single-day install record climbing from 22 to 113.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: 585 MWh to 1 GWh in under five months is the concrete year-end milestone to hold the company to.
insights.locator: It’s now deployed 585 MWh of storage

insights.claim: Base launched 'Base Energy' in April 2026, a battery-free electricity plan with guaranteed below-market rates for renters and apartment dwellers, and it reached more than 14,000 members within three months, pushing total membership above 30,000.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A capital-light channel that grew to nearly half of total membership in one quarter, monetizing the fleet's hedge value with no new hardware while serving as top-of-funnel.
insights.locator: In April, the company launched Base Energy

insights.claim: The retail electricity thesis is that a battery fleet physically substitutes for financial hedges: retailers are structurally short power and pay option premiums, while a battery fleet is long power, so combining them cuts risk and lets the savings be passed through as lower customer rates.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Explains how Base can sustainably undercut incumbent retail electric providers without subsidizing — the cost edge comes from replacing hedging premium with owned physical assets.
insights.quote: “The hedge is a financial battery,” as Jared described it. “The battery is a technical hedge.”
insights.locator: Selling electricity in a deregulated market

insights.claim: The homebuilder channel converts unusually well: Lennar accounted for roughly 2,500 homes, about 30% of Base's 2025 installations, and by March 2026 Base was available in 77 Lennar communities with a take rate above 65%.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A 65%+ attach rate at the point of home sale is the cheapest acquisition channel in the model and a template other national builders may replicate.
insights.locator: Lennar accounted for roughly 2,500 homes

insights.claim: Regulated utility partnerships went from a couple percent of Base's business in 2025 to 58% of July 2026 installs, growing from a single Bandera Electric Cooperative pilot into five larger partnerships totaling 220 MW.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: This directly resolves the biggest bear case an investor had voiced — that the model only works in deregulated markets — and unlocks the majority of the US that is regulated.
insights.locator: That initial Bandera pilot has turned into five larger

insights.claim: Utility partnerships deliver near-zero customer acquisition cost: roughly 5% of the addressable market signs up simply from the utility sending an email, though only after a multi-month or multi-year enterprise sales cycle to land the partnership.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: CAC should fall structurally as the mix shifts toward utilities, showing up as improving contribution margin even with flat hardware costs.
insights.quote: “You get like 5% of the addressable market signed up just by the utility sending an email. It’s a free CAC. I love it.”
insights.locator: From a go to market motion, the utility world is quite simple

insights.claim: Base monetizes the identical battery three different ways depending on market structure: owning the asset and selling electricity as a retail electric provider in deregulated Texas, deploying contracted fleets for co-ops and municipal utilities, and selling assets to investor-owned utilities via build-transfer contracts so the IOU can rate-base them and earn an allowed return while paying Base for software and services.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Business-model flexibility, not technology, is what makes national expansion possible — and the IOU build-transfer path turns Base into a capital-light software and services vendor in regulated states.
insights.locator: There are different types of utilities

insights.claim: The El Paso Electric partnership required installing 10 MW behind one constrained substation — roughly 10% of all homes behind it — to defer capacity upgrades, and Base finished two weeks early with one-third of the neighborhood signing up, executed largely by two marketing interns knocking doors in 104-degree heat.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Proves the highest-value utility use case — geographically targeted non-wires alternatives that defer capex — is operationally achievable, which is where regulated utilities will pay the most.
insights.locator: In El Paso, we had to deploy 10MW of batteries

insights.claim: Utility demand has inverted from Base chasing partnerships to large investor-owned utilities calling Base for help, a shift the CEO says did not exist fifteen months earlier, and Base's pitch is that most utility problems are coordination problems spanning generation, transmission, storage and retail simultaneously.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Inbound from IOUs is the leading indicator for regulated-market expansion; the first named IOU build-transfer contract outside Texas would be the confirming catalyst.
insights.quote: “All the big utilities are calling us and they’re saying, ‘Please help us,’ basically,”
insights.locator: When I spoke with Zach, he was on his way out

insights.claim: Base chose Illinois as its second market for structural reasons: roughly 4 million single-family homes, a deregulated market, the newly signed Clean and Reliable Grid Affordability Act (SB 25) establishing a 3 GW storage target by 2030, and residential battery access to PJM's high-priced wholesale capacity market.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: State storage mandates plus wholesale capacity market access form the checklist for where distributed storage expands next — a screen for predicting the third and fourth markets.
insights.locator: Illinois is large, with roughly 4 million single-family homes

insights.claim: Illinois offers a revenue stream Texas does not: time-varying distribution rates and aging infrastructure let Base get paid for relieving stress on local wires, a value stream it cannot currently monetize in deregulated Texas.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Revenue stacks differ materially by market, so distributed storage economics must be modeled state by state rather than as one national unit economic.
insights.locator: PJM’s high capacity prices make stored power

insights.claim: ComEd's all-in residential rate has jumped to 17.07¢/kWh, roughly 90% above the ~9¢/kWh level of 2021, which is why the Chicago pitch leads with affordability while the Texas pitch leads with reliability.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A 90% five-year retail rate increase in a major metro is simultaneously the demand driver for distributed storage and a mounting political risk for PJM-area utilities.
insights.locator: ComEd, the utility that covers Chicago

insights.claim: Storm-driven local news coverage is the most efficient demand catalyst: after July 27, 2026 storms cut power to more than 530,000 ComEd customers and the Chicago Tribune ran a favorable feature the next morning, 1,437 Chicagoland leads arrived in a single day — five times the previous best — with 172 signing that day against a prior daily record of 90.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Demand is event-driven and highly convex to grid failures, making outage frequency a real-time leading indicator for residential storage sales.
insights.locator: Then on July 27th, storms knocked out power

insights.claim: Base's policy team helped pass Texas SB1252 in August 2025, barring municipalities from amending the National Electrical Code or regulating installation of residential energy backup systems, making Texas the only state where the state itself controls permitting — while Chicagoland's 500-plus permitting jurisdictions put Base back to negotiating with individual inspectors.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Capturing the permitting layer is a replicable, high-ROI moat; track whether similar language lands in the federal permitting bill moving through Congress, since it would compress deployment costs nationally.
insights.quote: “if you think about Base as a machine that eats complexity and turns it into moats.”
insights.locator: Then, Base ate complexity and turned it into law

insights.claim: Data centers paying top dollar for electricians on short-term projects are now Base's main hiring challenge, forcing it to compete on benefits, 401k and equity rather than wages as it hires roughly 50 people in Chicagoland by year-end.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Skilled electrical labor is a shared bottleneck between AI datacenter buildout and distributed energy — a wage-inflation signal that raises delivered costs across both sectors.
insights.locator: Hiring electricians used to be a huge bottleneck

themes.theme: Pointing the Cannon at AI Compute

insights.claim: Base's stated next act is to reorient the entire company around AI infrastructure in two directions — bringing power to the compute and bringing compute to the power — with the CEO saying the result should be the largest energy technology company ever and perhaps the world's largest company.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Much of the $13B mark is optionality on this pivot; a concrete distributed-compute product announcement is the catalyst that would validate or deflate it.
insights.quote: “So now, we’re taking this Capability Cannon and we’re pointing it at the infrastructure buildout, and we’re going to do it in two broad ways: one is bringing the power to the compute, and two is bringing the compute to the power.”
insights.locator: While it’s a bit too early to share specifics

insights.claim: The technical argument for distributed compute is a spiderweb-and-sand analogy: a single large centralized load is like a rock that breaks the web wherever you place it, while the same hundreds of megawatts spread as sand across nodes with local grid headroom lets far more compute connect far more quickly.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: If interconnection queues remain the binding constraint on the AI buildout, distributed compute co-located with residential storage becomes a credible alternative to powered-land hyperscale campuses.
insights.quote: so the spiderweb can hold a lot more sand
insights.locator: One thing that’s hard with large, centralized grid-scale loads

insights.claim: The logic pushing Base into compute is that fixing a shrinking portion of the grid is pointless: compute is becoming the dominant load and, described as the fastest-growing consumer of electricity ever, is a major factor that could make the grid unhealthy.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Frames AI load growth as an existential requirement rather than an optional opportunity for any grid business — a lens for evaluating every utility and grid-tech position.
insights.quote: “And what is the power grid for? Increasingly, it’s for driving compute.”
insights.locator: The mission is to fix the grid

insights.claim: The author concedes Base would not be first to decentralized compute — Tesla did residential batteries earlier and Base outgrew it anyway — arguing the transferable advantages are hardware manufacturing, home installation logistics, and the ability to operate a distributed network as a single asset, rather than the idea itself.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: The bet is execution capability over novelty, which is the counter to any 'the incumbent already tried this' objection when sizing hardware entrants.
insights.locator: Base is not the first company to think about doing decentralized compute
